qualifications: This claim is grounded in the Ruiqi Hanji sequence through Hanji 191 and remains source-scoped to that interpretation of early Western Han founding.
Hanji 191 preserves the Zhou Bo/Fan Kuai conflict over Chen Xi's death rather than resolving it.
claims.statement: The early-Han sequence shows victory turning into governance only through family order, capital choice, exit management, reward ranking, ritual hierarchy, frontier containment, [[HanXiongnuHeqinPolicy|heqin]] diplomacy, vassal rollback, investigation-triggered rebellion risk, and finally the failure of personal trust in [[LuWan|Lu Wan]]'s Yan kingship.

qualifications: The Huainan branch is source-scoped; Xiao He's advice is investigation-first, but Ying Bu reads the inquiry through the prior deaths of Han Xin and Peng Yue.
The Yan branch is later-stage: Lu Wan has already hedged through Chen Xi and Xiongnu channels before summons and inspection expose the crisis.
claims.statement: Early Han vassal control has a feedback risk: accusations, summons, and investigations meant to manage autonomous powerholders can make exposed rulers interpret court procedure as a prelude to elimination, turning private access scandals or covert hedge behavior into rebellion triggers.

qualifications: The Yan case is coercive suppression, while the Nanyue case is frontier recognition; they share separation and incorporation logic but not the same legal status.
The South Sea king note is source-scoped as a possible nominal title rather than proof of effective Nanhai control.
claims.statement: Early Han governance can detach people or territory from a ruler without immediate full absorption: Liu Bang uses [[PoliticalSurrenderCascade|pardon and rank signaling]] to peel Yan officials away from Lu Wan, while [[RecognitionBackedFrontierDiplomacy]] keeps [[Nanyue]] inside Han hierarchy through title recognition despite unresolved control boundaries.

qualifications: The Qin and Warring States paragraphs support strong administrative capacity, while also warning that effective control can produce legitimacy and personal-survival costs.
claims.statement: State capacity appears as enforceable controls over appointments, territory, households, standards, symbols, and punishment, but [[PowerExitTrap|exit traps]] and backlash show that control does not automatically create social support.

qualifications: These sources are not one institutional lineage; they use literature and history to expose recurring governance problems around honor, truth, reputation, and political conditions.
claims.statement: Several cultural-history sources treat institutions as procedures for unstable status problems: duels, trials, political face, public moral performance, exile, and speed all turn private conflict into rule-bound or stage-bound behavior.

qualifications: The same rule-making that creates markets or accountability can also burden speech, access, or platform competition.
claims.statement: Regulation shapes markets by making costs, demand, and liability legible, from [[EmbodiedCarbonBuildingCode|building-carbon rules]] and low-carbon material sourcing to AI liability, satellite connectivity competition, physical-book platform bridges, and child-safety/privacy tradeoffs.

qualifications: The sports case is a micro-strategy analogy, while prediction markets raise broader regulatory and public-trust questions.
claims.statement: Whether in penalties or election markets, rule design has to manage predictability and information: better data is useful only when it preserves [[StrategicUnpredictability|strategic unpredictability]] or limits gambling, insider, and public-trust risks.

qualifications: These are heterogeneous cases; their shared point is that infrastructure and distribution choices create political effects even when framed as technical, commercial, or symbolic.
claims.statement: Infrastructure power becomes governance pressure when chip controls, data-center costs, assistant distribution, ideological talent pipelines, elections, sports bodies, and climate symbols shape who pays, who gets access, and who can set public narratives.

qualifications: The investment paragraph is about portfolio discipline, while the banking and AML paragraphs emphasize institutional trust and compliance exposure.
claims.statement: Finance governance links state capacity to user-level risk: accounting, banking, currency, AML, KYC, cross-border transfers, and investment constraints all determine what economic activity can be trusted, audited, or safely accessed.

qualifications: The Minnan case is long-run regional commercial infrastructure; the East Star Airlines case is a modern private-airline fragility case.
claims.statement: Enterprise growth depends on aligned public and private infrastructure: ports, diaspora remittances, manufacturing clusters, airline regulation, aircraft finance, local-government support, and cash discipline can amplify or break founder force.

qualifications: The claim joins older ownership structures, AI governance, operating culture, and founder-brand cases under the narrower question of how trust survives pressure.
claims.statement: Trust and mission are governance assets only when protected by structures: customer reliability, private standards, benefit trusts, stewardship ownership, AI alignment governance, post-acquisition identity, greenhushing, and growth pace all show that values can attract pressure as well as loyalty.

qualifications: This is source-scoped to the Ruiqi interpretation of the 197 CE cluster around Chen Deng, Chen Gui, Lu Bu, Guangling, Liu Chong, Luo Jun, Yuan Shu, Yuan Shao, He Kui, Xu Chu, and Yang Biao.
Hanji 1016 supports the title-legitimacy and marriage-exposure precondition; it does not by itself fully explain Yuan Shu's later collapse.
Hanji 1017's modern extension from light switching to jobs, marriage, friends, and investing is treated as source-scoped analogy rather than direct institutional evidence.
Hanji 1018 supports an interest-structure claim, not a complete biography of Lu Bu, Chen Deng, or Yuan Shu.
Hanji 1019 treats Chen state's order as dependent on a paired ruler-minister arrangement, so it supports fragility rather than a general claim that local refuge systems always fail.
It does not clear Cao Cao of coercive court control; the Kong Rong, Xun Yu, and Man Chong branch instead shows that harsh command still needs public legitimacy and evidentiary limits.
claims.statement: Hanji 1016-1020 frame late-Han state capacity as title legitimacy, character reading, staged local alignment, interest reading, coalition control, and talent retention: [[YuanShu]]'s unsupported imperial name becomes a [[MingqiLegitimacy]] liability, while [[ChenGui]] blocks [[MarriageAllianceWarExposure]] for [[Xuzhou]] by refusing pressure through [[ChenDeng]] and reversing [[LyuBu]]'s marriage route through [[HanYinLateHan]]; the same Han-court order can still appoint [[YuanShao]] through [[KongRong]]. Hanji 1017-1018 then have Chen Deng and Chen Gui identify Lü Bu's [[QingYuQuJiu]] risk, convert [[GuanglingCommandery]] into a Cao-aligned base under [[PoliticalSurvivalFirst]] and [[XingshiqingStrategicAssessment]], and read Lu Bu and Yuan Shu's incentives; Lü Bu can flip Han Xian and Yang Feng through [[InterestStructuredAllianceFragility]] but cannot turn [[GaoShun]]'s disciplined loyalty into durable capacity, [[LiuChongChenKing]] and [[LuoJun]] make [[ChenStateLateHan]] a refuge that [[ZhangKaiAssassin]] can decapitate for Yuan Shu, and [[CaoCao]] grows by absorbing [[HeKui]] and [[XuChu]] while [[YangBiao]]'s case shows prosecution near [[EmperorXianOfHan]] remains constrained by old-Han prestige and evidence.

summary: Governance in the current corpus is a set of translation mechanisms: conquest becomes founding order, legal doctrine becomes enforceable administration, local refuge becomes person-dependent security, public symbols become legitimacy, markets become rule-bound information systems, and private trust becomes a governing asset. Hanji 1016-1020 widen the late-Han branch from title legitimacy into staged family survival and coalition control: Yuan Shu's imperial name is a liability without capacity and recognition, Chen Gui blocks the Yuan Shu-Lu Bu marriage route to protect Xuzhou and the Chen family, Chen Deng and Chen Gui diagnose Lu Bu's light switching, turn Guangling into a Cao-aligned base, read dependency, vanity, legitimacy, and spoils more accurately than stronger military actors, and expose why Lu Bu can exploit a brittle Yuan Shu coalition but cannot make Gao Shun's disciplined capacity durable. Hanji 1019 adds a later local-order case in which Liu Chong and Luo Jun make Chen state a refuge, but Yuan Shu's use of false surrender exposes how quickly a leadership-pair system can be decapitated. Hanji 1020 extends that branch: reading momentum, holding trust, and retaining talent decide whether Yuan Shu's formal ambition collapses while Cao Cao's harsh but talent-absorbing coalition grows, though Yang Biao's case shows prestige and evidence can still constrain court prosecution. Hanji 191 sharpens the early-Han side: even personal intimacy cannot dissolve different-surname king risk, so Lu Wan's Yan crisis turns trust into investigation, frontier hedging, military pressure, and pardon-based separation of a ruler from his officials. The topic also keeps the liabilities visible: frontier defeats force diplomacy, autonomous vassal rollback can make investigation itself dangerous, hard controls can backfire, platform and AI rules can burden rights, financial compliance shifts risk onto users, and mission-led organizations still face capital, burnout, and stewardship pressure.
